subtitle: How a self-taught Canadian entrepreneur turned curiosity, compassion and a pay-what-you-can mindset into a tech company that leaves no one behind.

excerpt: Most of us only think about our computer when it stops working. For Alejandro Calle, founder of Tech In A Tux, that moment of panic is where the real work begins.
content:
Executive Spotlight 2026

Most of us only think about our computer when it stops working. For Alejandro Calle, that moment of panic is where the job begins. It might be a laptop holding years of family photos, a business owner locked out of the system that pays the bills, or a first-time user staring at a device that feels impossible to understand. Behind every one of those problems is a person who needs patience, honesty and respect. That belief is the foundation of Tech In A Tux, the Canadian tech support company he built to make technology work for people.

Self-Taught and Curious: How Alejandro Calle Got Started

Alejandro's story begins with a question that never went away: how do things actually work? As a young person fascinated by computers, he was never satisfied with simply using technology. He wanted to know what was happening behind the screen, how to track down a problem, and how to make something better.

There was no roadmap and no instructor pointing the way. He learned through research, experimentation, plenty of mistakes and countless hours of figuring things out alone. Technology also moves fast. Just when one system feels familiar, another arrives, so staying adaptable became part of the job.

What he gained was worth more than any single skill. Being self-taught taught him to think critically, solve problems on his own and treat learning as something that never ends. It also gave him a conviction he now shares with others: you don't need a traditional path to build something meaningful, and you don't need to know everything before you start.

“ Don't wait until you know everything to begin. — Alejandro Calle, Founder & CEO, Tech In A Tux

Tech In A Tux: Affordable Tech Support Built Around People

Tech In A Tux was founded on a simple mission: make tech support accessible to all, regardless of financial situation. Alejandro saw a world where technology had become essential to communication, education and work, yet millions of people felt left behind because it was confusing, expensive or intimidating.

His answer was a company that offers professional, reliable help without judgment. Even the name says it: professionalism and personality in an industry that can feel cold and impersonal. Whether a client needs a basic computer repair, data recovery, a new website or a full digital solution, the standard is the same.

The pay-what-you-can approach comes from a plain observation: a broken computer doesn't care about your income. It can put a job, a course or a connection with family at risk. Alejandro is also realistic about running a business. Larger projects need fair pricing, and a company that can't sustain itself can't help anyone for long. To him, profit and generosity aren't opposites. A healthy business simply has more room to give back.

Honesty shapes the daily work too. If something doesn't need replacing, he won't suggest replacing it. If a cheaper fix exists, clients hear about it first. The goal is never the biggest sale, only the right solution.

“ It's not about selling the most expensive service. It's about recommending the right solution. — Alejandro Calle

The Moments That Matter Most

Ask Alejandro about his most memorable work and he rarely names the most complicated job. He describes the relief on someone's face when a problem that felt hopeless is finally fixed. Often that means recovering family photos or documents a person feared were gone for good. Technically, it's a hardware diagnosis or a software fix. To the client, it's protecting something that can't be replaced.

Helping a small business get online works the same way. A website is never just a handful of pages. It can represent a dream, years of hard work and a first chance to reach new customers. Experiences like these taught him that tech support is really about people, and the words he values most are the simple ones: thank you, you've made my life so much easier.

Teaching Technology to a Global Community

Alejandro's reach goes well beyond his local clients. His online channel has grown to more than 200,000 subscribers and over 60 million views, a community of people from many backgrounds and countries. What matters to him isn't the numbers but the value behind them.

He believes technology doesn't have to be complicated to be interesting, and learning doesn't have to be boring to work. Most people don't want jargon. They want someone to explain things clearly, show them how something works and help them feel more confident. Whether he's presenting a technical idea in a fun way or exploring emerging tech, the aim is to make people curious rather than intimidated.

The community has also taught him to listen. Some of his most useful feedback comes from people simply describing what they struggle with, and that has made him a better technician, communicator, creator and entrepreneur.

Leadership and “The Secret To Living Is Giving”

Building a company mostly on your own means wearing every hat. Alejandro is the technician, the customer service team, the marketer and the person who makes the financial calls. Balancing those roles, and accepting that he can't do everything at once, has taught him patience and prioritization. He picks decisions that support long-term growth over short-term excitement.

His idea of leadership is just as grounded. It isn't about having every answer. It's about taking responsibility, staying willing to learn and leading by example.

That outlook sums up the philosophy he lives by: “The Secret To Living Is Giving.” Giving doesn't always mean money. It can be sharing knowledge, offering time or simply being there when someone needs help. Something that takes him ten minutes to explain can save another person hours of frustration, and the idea keeps him tied to the reason he started.

“ Success isn't simply about how much money a business makes. It's also about what that business makes possible for others. — Alejandro Calle

AI, the Digital Divide and a More Human Future

Looking ahead, Alejandro believes we are entering one of the most exciting stretches in the history of technology. Artificial intelligence and automation now give small businesses and individuals abilities that once took a whole team. He takes the risks seriously too, from privacy and cybersecurity to misinformation and a widening digital divide.

His worry isn't that technology is moving too fast. It's that people get left behind when no one makes the effort to teach and support them. That's where he sees Tech In A Tux going: more services, responsible use of AI, more educational content, and steady guidance for people and businesses navigating a digital world. He pictures a trusted resource and a learning community that helps people welcome innovation with confidence.

What he hopes to leave behind is more than a successful company. It's a positive example that encourages others to share what they know, follow their passions and help people along the way.

Visionary Perspective • Quotes from Alejandro Calle

“Let's Make Tech Support Accessible To All, regardless of their financial situation.”

“Don't wait until you know everything to begin.”

“It's not about selling the most expensive service. It's about recommending the right solution.”

“Success isn't simply about how much money a business makes. It's also about what that business makes possible for others.”

“The future of technology shouldn't just be smarter. It should be more human.”

title: Jensen Huang and Nvidia: How the AI Chip Industry Got Its Defining Leader
shortTitle: The Man Behind the AI Chips
subtitle: From a 1993 start-up bet to the first $5 trillion company, here is how Nvidia's CEO built the engine of the AI era, and what could still slow it down.
author: The Empire Insight Editorial Board
quotes: Nvidia didn't just ride the AI wave. It spent years building the road the wave would travel on.
A moat made of software is harder to cross than a moat made of silicon.
In AI, the chip gets the headlines, but the ecosystem wins the decade.
excerpt: Nvidia went from selling graphics cards to powering the AI boom. Here is how Jensen Huang built the company, why its software moat is so strong, and the risks it still faces.
content:
Executive Spotlight 2026

Plenty of CEOs get described as visionaries. Very few get to watch their company become the engine under an entire technology era. Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of Nvidia, is one of the exceptions. A company that once sold graphics cards to PC gamers is now the name most often attached to the AI boom, and the chips it designs sit inside the data centers that train and run today's biggest AI models. This is the story of how that happened, why Nvidia is so hard to catch, and what could still go wrong.

From a Denny's Booth to the Center of the AI Industry

Nvidia's origin story is almost too neat, but it is well documented. In 1993, Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem started the company with a bet that three-dimensional graphics would become a mass-market product. The early days were scrappy. The company nearly ran out of money more than once, and the founders were building for a market that barely existed yet.

Huang's own path was not a straight line either. Born in Taiwan, he moved to the United States as a child, studied electrical engineering at Oregon State University, then earned a master's degree at Stanford. Before Nvidia he worked at LSI Logic and AMD, which gave him a close look at how chips actually get designed, sold and supported. That mix of engineering depth and commercial instinct is a big part of why Nvidia survived the years when graphics was a brutal, crowded business.

The breakthrough product arrived in 1999 with the GeForce 256, which Nvidia marketed as the world's first GPU. It was built for games, but the architecture had a hidden strength: a GPU does thousands of small calculations at the same time. That turned out to be exactly what scientists, and later AI researchers, needed.

“ Nvidia didn't just ride the AI wave. It spent years building the road the wave would travel on. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

The Quiet Bet That Changed Everything: CUDA

If you want to understand why Nvidia leads, don't start with the chips. Start with software. In the mid-2000s Nvidia released CUDA, a programming platform that let developers use GPUs for general-purpose computing, not just graphics. At the time, plenty of investors saw it as a costly side project. Nvidia was adding silicon features and engineering effort for customers who didn't yet exist.

Then came 2012. A team of researchers trained an image-recognition network called AlexNet on Nvidia GPUs and blew past the competition. Deep learning suddenly looked practical, and the researchers had already been using CUDA. A generation of AI developers grew up writing code for Nvidia hardware, and the libraries, tutorials and tools that followed made it the default choice.

That is the real moat. Anyone can, in theory, design a fast chip. It is much harder to replace the software ecosystem that millions of developers already know, trust and have built their careers around. Switching away from Nvidia is not just a hardware decision. It means rewriting code, retraining people and accepting risk on a deadline.

How Nvidia Became a Full-Stack AI Company

Under Huang, Nvidia stopped thinking of itself as a chip supplier years ago. Today it sells whole systems: GPUs, high-speed networking, interconnects, server designs, and the software to tie them together. The pitch to customers is simple. Instead of buying parts and hoping they work well together, buy a data center that was designed as one machine.

The product cadence is relentless. After the Hopper generation came Blackwell, and the next platform, Vera Rubin, is already central to the company's roadmap. At its GTC conference in 2026, Huang talked about enormous demand for Blackwell and Rubin systems stretching through 2027, with a figure of around a trillion dollars in orders and opportunity. Treat any number like that as a forecast rather than a guarantee, but it tells you how the company sees the next two years.

Nvidia also became the first publicly traded company to pass a $5 trillion market value, a milestone it reached in October 2025. For comparison, only a few years earlier a company worth a tenth of that was considered enormous. The valuation moves around daily, so we won't pin it to a single number here, but the direction of travel is clear: investors treat Nvidia as a proxy for the entire AI buildout.

The Leadership Style Behind the Leather Jacket

Huang has a recognizable public persona. The black leather jacket, the long keynotes, the habit of talking to engineers as if they were the stars of the show. But the more interesting part is how he runs the place. Nvidia is known for a flat structure where Huang reportedly keeps a very large number of direct reports and favors open discussion over tidy org charts.

He is also known for thinking in long cycles. Nvidia spent years investing in CUDA, in networking, in AI software, long before the revenue showed up. Many leaders say they think long term. Few have the stomach to keep spending on something for a decade while analysts ask when it will pay off.

It would be a mistake, though, to tell this as a pure hero story. Plenty of Nvidia's success came from timing, from rivals that moved slowly, and from a market that suddenly needed exactly what the company had spent years building. Huang would probably be the first to admit luck played a role. The skill was being ready when it did.

“ A moat made of software is harder to cross than a moat made of silicon. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

The Competition Is Real, and It Is Getting Serious

Nvidia's lead is large, but it isn't safe. Several of its biggest customers are also its most determined challengers. Google builds its own TPU chips, Amazon has Trainium and Inferentia, Microsoft and Meta are developing custom silicon, and companies like Broadcom help big cloud providers design chips tailored to their own workloads. AMD, meanwhile, keeps pushing its Instinct accelerators and has won some high-profile deployments.

Why would customers spend billions building their own chips? Control and cost. When you run AI at enormous scale, shaving a few percentage points off the price of every calculation matters. Custom chips can also be tuned to a specific model in ways general-purpose GPUs can't.

Nvidia's answer has been to move faster and bundle more. By selling complete systems and keeping its software ecosystem central, it makes the cost of leaving higher. Whether that is enough over a ten-year horizon is the central question for anyone watching this industry.

The Risks Nobody Should Ignore

  • Supply chain limits. Nvidia designs chips but relies on TSMC to manufacture them and on advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory that remain tight. Great demand means little if the parts can't be built.
  • Geopolitics and export controls. Rules on selling advanced chips to China have repeatedly reshaped what Nvidia can sell and where. Policy shifts can erase or reopen a major market with very little warning.
  • Customer concentration. A handful of giant cloud companies buy a large share of the output. If their spending slows, Nvidia feels it quickly.
  • Circular financing worries. Nvidia has invested in AI labs and cloud partners that then buy its hardware. Critics argue this can inflate demand signals. Supporters say it is simply how an ecosystem grows.
  • Power and infrastructure. AI data centers consume huge amounts of electricity. Grid capacity and permitting may end up limiting growth as much as chips do.

None of these is a prediction of failure. They are the pressure points that a company this central has to manage every quarter.

What Nvidia's Rise Means for Everyone Else

You don't have to own Nvidia stock to feel its influence. It shapes how quickly new AI products reach the market, what they cost to run, and which countries and companies can afford to compete. When GPU supply is tight, startups wait in line and prices climb. When supply loosens, experimentation speeds up.

For businesses, the practical lesson is to avoid assuming infrastructure will always be cheap or available. Plan for access to computing power the way you would plan for any critical supply. For students and early-career engineers, the lesson is that the boring layer underneath the flashy apps, meaning chips, systems and software, is where an enormous amount of value is being created.

And for Huang himself? The challenge now is different from the one he faced in 1993. Back then the question was survival. Today the question is stewardship: keeping a company this important innovative, honest about its risks, and useful to the people who depend on it.

What Huang Gets Right, and Where Critics Push Back

Admirers point to a few habits that set Huang apart. He treats failure as information, he keeps his product roadmap public so customers can plan around it, and he spends as much time on software and partnerships as on silicon. Nvidia's engineers have also been unusually willing to build things the market didn't ask for yet, which is how they ended up ready when AI demand arrived.

Critics raise fair counterpoints. Some argue that Nvidia's pricing power leaves customers feeling trapped. Others worry about how much of the global AI economy now hangs on a single supplier, and whether that concentration is healthy. There is also a more philosophical debate about whether today's huge data center spending will earn its money back. Nobody knows yet, including the people writing the checks. A balanced view is that Nvidia has earned its position through real engineering, while also benefiting from a boom that may not last at this pace forever.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Jensen Huang?

Jensen Huang is the co-founder, president and CEO of Nvidia, the company that designs the GPUs and AI systems used to train and run many of the world's leading AI models.

Why is Nvidia so dominant in AI chips?

Its GPUs are extremely good at parallel computing, and its CUDA software platform gives developers a mature ecosystem that is difficult and expensive to leave.

Who competes with Nvidia?

AMD is the closest traditional rival, while Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta are building custom chips, often with help from partners such as Broadcom.

What are the biggest risks to Nvidia?

Supply constraints in manufacturing and packaging, export restrictions, heavy reliance on a few large customers, and the possibility that AI spending slows.

Key Takeaways • Nvidia and the AI Chip Industry

Nvidia's real advantage is a software ecosystem built over nearly two decades, not just fast hardware.

The company now sells complete AI systems, which makes it harder for customers to switch.

Custom chips from big cloud providers are the most credible long-term challenge.

Manufacturing capacity, export rules and power supply are the main limits on growth.

Jensen Huang's biggest test now is stewardship, not survival.

Jensen Huang

Co-Founder & CEO, Nvidia Santa Clara, California, USA
1993 Nvidia Founded
$5T+ First to Cross (Oct 2025)
CUDA The Software Moat

Bottom Line: “In AI, the chip gets the headlines, but the ecosystem wins the decade.”

title: Elon Musk's Flying Car: What the Tesla Roadster Demo Really Showed
subtitle: Tesla's rocket-assisted Roadster left the ground in Texas. Here is what happened, why real flying cars are so hard, and what to watch before 2028.
author: The Empire Insight Editorial Board
quotes: A car that can hop is not the same thing as a car that can fly. Both can be impressive, and only one of them is a transport system.
The best way to judge a bold demo is to ask what the boring version looks like. Who certifies it, who insures it, and who fixes it?
A great demo is the start of the story, not the end of it.
excerpt: On October 15, 2026, Tesla's new Roadster briefly left the ground using SpaceX thrusters. Is it a real flying car, or an impressive stunt? We break down the facts.
content:
Tech Spotlight 2026

For about a hundred years, "where's my flying car?" has been the standard joke about the future. On October 15, 2026, Elon Musk tried to end the joke. At a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, a redesigned Tesla Roadster drove up a ramp, left the ground, flipped, and came back down on its wheels. Musk called it proof that flying cars are real. Skeptics called it a very expensive stunt. The honest answer sits somewhere in between, and it is more interesting than either camp admits.

What Actually Happened in Texas

The demo was livestreamed from a SpaceX facility, and the details matter. The Roadster used cold-gas thrusters developed with SpaceX, fed by ultra-high-pressure air tanks. In plain terms, it wasn't burning rocket fuel or spinning giant rotors. It released bursts of compressed air through nozzles to push itself off the ground.

Reports from the event describe the car driving along a ramp upside down, briefly lifting off, passing over a line of parked Tesla vehicles, and performing a flip before landing intact. There was no driver on board. Musk said that was "to make sure we don't kill anyone," and he was candid that success was not guaranteed beforehand. Tesla also claimed a zero-to-sixty time under one second, and coverage of the demo reported a measured 0.81 seconds.

Afterward, Musk posted that the future does have flying cars and told the audience that production is planned for 2028. He described the car as the product of Tesla and SpaceX working together.

“ A car that can hop is not the same thing as a car that can fly. Both can be impressive, and only one of them is a transport system. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

A Very Long Wait for the Roadster

To understand the reaction, you need the history. Tesla first showed a next-generation Roadster back in 2017, with deliveries promised for 2020. They didn't happen. For years the car became a running joke among Tesla watchers, a product that was always a little further away.

Late in 2025, Musk said the new version would get a demo that would be "unforgettable," and he hinted at SpaceX technology being involved. Dates slipped repeatedly through 2026. The latest delay pushed the event from an early October date, with Tesla citing high winds. So when the car finally moved, the relief among fans was real, and so was the cynicism from everyone who had heard the promise before.

Is It a Flying Car? Here Is How to Think About It

A fair test is to ask what people actually mean by a flying car. Most imagine a vehicle you can drive to the end of your street, take off from, fly across a city, and land at your destination. That requires sustained flight, which needs lift, power, stability, navigation, and a safe way to fail.

The Roadster demonstration showed something different: short, controlled bursts of thrust. Compressed air stores limited energy, so it is excellent for a dramatic hop and poor for going anywhere. Several outlets pointed out that the vehicle is better described as a car that can briefly leave the ground than as a conventional flying car. That doesn't make the engineering trivial. Getting a car's worth of mass to move precisely, land safely on its tires, and survive the stress is hard. It just isn't the same problem as cruising at altitude.

Why Real Flying Cars Are So Hard

The physics problem comes first. Cars are heavy, wide, and designed to stay planted on the road. Aircraft are light, aerodynamic, and designed to stay in the sky. Combine both jobs in one body and you usually get compromises in each. Weight kills range. Wings or rotors complicate parking and crash safety. Batteries still store far less energy than the same weight of liquid fuel.

Then comes the rulebook. A road vehicle in the United States answers to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. An aircraft answers to the Federal Aviation Administration. A flying car lands in both worlds, and each regulator has strict, different expectations about crash protection, certification, pilot training and maintenance. Musk himself said the Roadster was "not necessarily a safety-optimized car," which is the kind of sentence regulators read very carefully.

Finally there is the everyday question nobody likes to ask. What happens when thousands of drivers with no pilot training are allowed to take off over cities? Traffic jams are annoying. Mid-air ones are not.

The Companies Already Trying

Musk isn't alone, and some rivals have taken a less theatrical route. Companies such as Joby and Archer are building electric air taxis that don't pretend to be cars at all. They take off vertically, fly a set route, and are designed from the start to meet aviation rules. Alef Aeronautics in California has pursued a road-capable vehicle with a vertical flight design and has received special airworthiness approval for testing. Klein Vision's AirCar in Slovakia, a car that converts into a plane with wings, has completed flight tests.

The difference is the target. Most of these companies aim at carefully regulated, limited use. Tesla's pitch, at least as spoken on stage, is more cultural: a stunning, fast, desirable car that happens to hint at the sci-fi future. That's classic Musk. He sells the dream first and lets the engineering catch up.

Genius, Gimmick, or Both?

Reaction to the demo split quickly. Fans saw a promise kept after nearly a decade. Some investors read it as a mood-lifting spectacle for a company that has been leaning heavily on future technologies like autonomy and robots. One well-known tech investor reportedly described it as an engineering flex with little commercial value beyond impressing rivals. Others shared jokes about flying cars crashing into billboards.

Here is our read. The demo almost certainly has marketing value, and Tesla has always understood that attention is currency. It also seems to have real technical interest, because it showed that SpaceX-style propulsion can be packaged into a road car. But the distance between a controlled stunt on a private test site and a product that thousands of customers can use safely is huge. Remember too that a 2028 production date is a promise, and Tesla's track record with dates is mixed.

“ The best way to judge a bold demo is to ask what the boring version looks like. Who certifies it, who insures it, and who fixes it? — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

What to Watch Between Now and 2028

  • Regulatory signals. Does the NHTSA or FAA say anything about how a thruster-assisted car would be classified?
  • Safety data. Independent testing, crash analysis and clear limits on where thrusters can be used.
  • The price and the spec sheet. Final pricing, range, and what the production car can actually do compared with the demo vehicle.
  • Real-world use cases. Is the thruster package a track feature, a party trick, or something genuinely useful?
  • Delivery dates. The Roadster has slipped before, so schedule updates will say a lot.

The Bigger Picture

Whatever happens to the Roadster, the demo says something about where transportation might go. Electric motors, better batteries, lightweight materials, and software-controlled stability are making unusual vehicles more plausible than they were twenty years ago. A fully mainstream flying car may still be a long way off, but the building blocks are improving.

For now, the safest conclusion is also the most grounded one. October 15 was a genuinely striking engineering moment, and it did not deliver the flying car of the cartoons. It delivered a very fast electric car that can briefly defy gravity. If the 2028 plan holds, we will find out how much that is worth to the people who can afford it.

How Cold-Gas Thrusters Work, in Plain English

Think of a balloon you let go of without tying it. The air rushes out one way, and the balloon shoots the other way. A cold-gas thruster follows the same basic principle, only with strong materials, high pressure and careful control. Compressed gas is stored in a sturdy tank, and valves release it through nozzles aimed in specific directions.

The upside is simplicity and precision. There is no fire, no complicated combustion, and the thrust can be switched on and off quickly, which is why spacecraft use similar systems for small adjustments. The downside is energy. Compressed air carries far less energy than fuel, so the effect is brief. That is why a demo can look spectacular while still being very far from a sustained journey across town.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Elon Musk really unveil a flying car?

Tesla unveiled a redesigned Roadster on October 15, 2026, that briefly lifted off the ground using SpaceX-developed cold-gas thrusters. Many outlets noted that it is not a conventional flying car capable of sustained flight.

How does the Tesla Roadster fly?

It uses cold-gas thrusters powered by high-pressure compressed air, which release short bursts of thrust rather than burning fuel or using wings or rotors.

When will the flying Tesla Roadster be released?

Musk said production is planned for 2028. Tesla has delayed this car before, so the date should be treated as a target.

Is the new Roadster legal to fly?

The demo ran on a private test site with no driver on board. Road and aviation regulators have not published rules for a vehicle like this, so legality remains an open question.

Key Takeaways • Elon Musk's Flying Car

The Roadster demo on October 15, 2026, used SpaceX cold-gas thrusters to leave the ground briefly.

It showed controlled hops and flips, not sustained flight, so it is not a conventional flying car.

Regulation, weight, battery limits and safety are the real obstacles to flying cars.

Musk's 2028 production target is a promise, and this car has a history of delays.

A great demo is the start of the story, not the end of it.

Elon Musk

CEO, Tesla & SpaceX Texas, USA
Oct 15 2026 Roadster Demo
0.81s Reported 0-60 mph
2028 Planned Production

Bottom Line: “Impressive demo, unfinished product.”

title: Digital Transformation Trends: 7 Shifts Changing Business in Late 2026 and Beyond
subtitle: AI agents, data quality, zero-trust security and more: a practical look at the seven trends that matter, and how to choose the ones that fit your business.
author: The Empire Insight Editorial Board
quotes: Before you buy smarter software, make sure it has something smart to read.
Trust is becoming a technology feature. Companies that can explain what their systems do will win more than those that merely claim they are smart.
Choose fewer trends, finish more projects.
excerpt: Seven digital transformation trends are reshaping how companies work in late 2026. Here is what each means in practice, and a simple way to pick what applies to you.
content:
Business Insight 2026

Every year, someone publishes a list of digital transformation trends, and every year most of them read like the same list with the dates changed. This one is different in a small but important way. We're not going to tell you which buzzwords to chase. We're going to look at the seven shifts that are actually changing how companies run in late 2026, what each one means in practice, and where businesses of any size tend to trip. If you want a shorter definition of the term itself, our earlier primer on digital transformation covers it. Here, we're going deeper into what's next.

Why Trends Matter Less Than Timing

Here's a quiet truth about digital transformation. The technology is rarely the hard part. Most companies already have access to the same cloud platforms, the same AI tools and the same analytics software as their competitors. What separates the winners is the order in which they do things, and whether they do them in a way their people can actually absorb.

So treat the trends below as a menu, not a checklist. A forty-person logistics firm and a global bank can both benefit from them, but they should pick very different dishes.

Trend 1: AI Agents Move From Demo to Daily Work

The conversation has shifted from chatbots that answer questions to agents that complete tasks. An agent might read an incoming invoice, match it against a purchase order, flag a mismatch and draft an email to the supplier, all before a human opens their inbox. Many companies are now testing this kind of automation in finance, customer service, IT support and sales operations.

The catch is trust. An agent that is right ninety-five percent of the time is wonderful for drafting and risky for anything involving money or legal commitments. The smart pattern is to keep a person in the loop for decisions with real consequences and let the software handle the repetitive prep. Analysts have warned that a large share of early agent projects will stall, mostly because organizations automate processes that were already broken. Fix the workflow first. Then automate it.

Trend 2: Data Quality Becomes the Real AI Strategy

Every serious AI project eventually runs into the same wall. The model is clever, but the company's data is scattered across spreadsheets, old systems and departments that don't talk to each other. You can't build reliable AI on top of unreliable data.

That's why more businesses are investing in unglamorous work: cleaning customer records, agreeing on common definitions, and setting up clear ownership of who is responsible for what data. It isn't exciting to announce at a board meeting. It is, however, the difference between an AI tool people trust and one they quietly stop using.

“ Before you buy smarter software, make sure it has something smart to read. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

Trend 3: Cybersecurity Becomes a Design Choice

As companies connect more systems, vendors and remote workers, the old idea of a protected company network falls apart. More organizations are adopting a zero-trust approach, which simply means that no user or device is trusted by default and every request is verified. That usually involves multi-factor authentication, careful access controls, and monitoring that looks for unusual behavior.

AI adds a twist. The same technology that helps defenders spot threats also helps attackers write convincing phishing emails and clone voices. Training staff to pause and verify unexpected requests, especially anything involving payments or passwords, remains one of the cheapest and most effective defenses available.

Trend 4: Cloud Spending Gets Disciplined

The first wave of cloud adoption was about moving fast. The second wave is about paying attention. Many companies discovered that unmanaged cloud usage can quietly become one of their largest expenses, with forgotten servers and oversized plans running day and night.

A practice often called FinOps, short for financial operations, has grown out of this. It brings finance, engineering and business teams together so that everyone can see what cloud resources cost and what value they produce. Meanwhile, plenty of organizations are choosing a mix of public cloud, private systems and edge computing, putting each workload where it makes the most sense for cost, speed and data rules.

Trend 5: Low-Code Tools Put Builders Inside Every Department

Low-code and no-code platforms let people who aren't professional developers build simple apps and automations. A sales manager can create a lead tracker. An operations lead can build an approval workflow. When it works, it clears a backlog that would otherwise sit in the IT queue for months.

The risk is sprawl. If everyone builds their own tools with no oversight, a company can end up with hundreds of fragile apps that nobody owns, holding sensitive data nobody is guarding. The fix isn't to ban the tools. It's to set a few clear rules about what can be built, who reviews it and where the data lives.

Trend 6: The Employee Experience Gets Treated Like Customer Experience

For years, companies obsessed over making things easy for customers while staff struggled with clumsy internal systems. That is changing. Businesses now realize that slow approvals, confusing portals and too many logins cost real time and morale.

Good digital transformation asks a simple question: if a new hire had to complete this task on day one, would it make sense? Where the answer is no, there's probably a process worth redesigning. And training matters here more than almost anything. A modest tool people understand beats a powerful one they avoid.

Trend 7: Regulation and Responsible AI Move to the Front

Rules around data privacy and AI use are tightening in many regions. The European Union's AI Act is being phased in, and other governments are following with their own approaches. Even companies far from Europe may feel the effects if they serve customers or partners there.

The practical response is not panic but documentation. Know which AI systems you use, what data they touch, who is accountable for them and how you would explain their decisions to a customer or regulator. Businesses that build this discipline early will find it far easier than those scrambling later.

“ Trust is becoming a technology feature. Companies that can explain what their systems do will win more than those that merely claim they are smart. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

How to Choose What Applies to You

With seven trends on the table, the temptation is to try all of them. Please don't. A better approach is to ask three questions about each one.

  1. Does it solve a problem we actually have? If you can't name the pain point, skip it for now.
  2. Are our basics in place? Clean data, working security habits and trained people come before advanced tools.
  3. Can we test it small? Run a pilot with one team, measure the result, and only then expand.

If a trend fails the first question, it's noise for you, however loudly the industry is talking about it.

Common Mistakes That Quietly Sink Projects

  • Buying before defining. Choosing a platform before agreeing on the problem it should solve.
  • Ignoring the people. Rolling out a system without asking the staff who will use it every day.
  • Skipping measurement. Launching without a baseline, then having no way to tell whether things improved.
  • Treating it as a one-off. Digital transformation is ongoing. Tools change, habits drift, and processes need regular attention.

Looking Ahead to 2027

If there's a single theme running through all seven trends, it's that the technology is becoming easier to buy and harder to use well. The scarce resource is no longer access to software. It's judgment, clean data, good habits and people who understand how the pieces fit together.

That is good news for smaller businesses, because judgment doesn't require a big budget. A team that picks one problem, fixes the process, trains its people and measures the result can outperform a much larger rival that bought everything and finished nothing.

A Simple 90-Day Starter Plan

If all of this feels like a lot, here is a way to begin without a big budget or a consultant. In the first month, list your five most annoying recurring tasks and pick the one that wastes the most hours. Talk to the people who do it and write down each step exactly as it happens, mess and all.

In the second month, remove any steps that add nothing, then choose one tool to automate or simplify the rest. Run it with a small group. In the third month, measure time saved, errors avoided and how people feel about it, then decide whether to expand, adjust or stop. It sounds almost too modest, but this loop of define, simplify, pilot and measure is what most successful transformations look like up close.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the top digital transformation trends in 2026?

The most important are AI agents, a stronger focus on data quality, zero-trust cybersecurity, disciplined cloud cost management, low-code tools, better employee experience and responsible AI governance.

Is digital transformation only for large companies?

No. Small businesses often move faster because they have fewer layers of approval. The key is choosing a few tools that solve real problems.

Where should a company start with digital transformation?

Start with one clear problem, map how the work happens today, fix obvious flaws, and run a small pilot before scaling up.

Why do digital transformation projects fail?

Usually because of unclear goals, poor data, lack of training and resistance from people who were never consulted, rather than because of the technology itself.

Key Takeaways • Digital Transformation Trends

AI agents work best when a human stays in the loop for high-stakes decisions.

Clean, well-owned data is the foundation of any useful AI strategy.

Security, cost control and governance are now part of the design, not an afterthought.

Pick trends that solve a real problem, and test them small first.

Technology is easier to buy than ever, but judgment is still the scarce resource.

7 Key Trends
3 Questions to Filter Them
1 Problem to Start With

Bottom Line: “Choose fewer trends, finish more projects.”

title: Semiconductor Equipment Shortage: Why Chip Manufacturing Bottlenecks Are So Hard to Fix
subtitle: ASML, CoWoS packaging, high-bandwidth memory and long equipment lead times: why AI demand is outrunning the machines that make the chips.
author: The Empire Insight Editorial Board
quotes: You can print money faster than you can print a new chip factory.
A chip factory is a promise that takes years to keep.
The limit on AI is not ideas. It is how fast the world can build the machines that build the chips.
excerpt: The new chip squeeze is about advanced AI processors, memory and the machines that build them. Here is what is causing it, and when relief may arrive.
content:
Industry Insight 2026

When most people hear "chip shortage," they think of 2021, when car factories sat idle because of a missing part the size of a fingernail. The new squeeze is different, and in some ways it is harder to fix. This time the pinch is not in cheap, everyday chips. It sits in the most advanced corner of the industry, where AI processors, high-bandwidth memory and the machines that build them are all competing for the same limited capacity. Here is what's going on with the semiconductor equipment shortage, why chip manufacturing bottlenecks are so stubborn, and what it means for anyone who buys technology.

This Isn't the 2021 Shortage

The pandemic-era shortage was mostly about mature chips, the older, cheaper kind that run car electronics and appliances. Demand whipsawed, supply couldn't keep up, and the shortage eased once factories adjusted.

Today's pressure comes from artificial intelligence. Training and running large AI models takes huge numbers of advanced processors, and each one needs high-bandwidth memory and specialized packaging. Research firm Omdia has raised its 2026 forecast for global chip revenue sharply and says supply bottlenecks may persist into 2027, because AI demand is growing faster than factories can expand. The shortage is less like a traffic jam and more like a highway that was never built wide enough for the cars now using it.

Why Equipment Is the Hidden Choke Point

Here's the part that surprises people. You can't simply decide to build more chips. First you need a factory, which can cost tens of billions of dollars. Then you need machines to fill it, and those machines come from a small number of specialist companies with their own limits.

The headline name is ASML, the Dutch company that is the only supplier of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, the tools that print the finest circuit patterns on leading-edge chips. A single EUV system is enormous, extremely complex and costs hundreds of millions of dollars. It is assembled from parts supplied by a long chain of specialist firms, including mirrors, lasers and precision components that few companies in the world can make.

ASML has said it expects to ship more than sixty EUV systems in 2026, roughly a quarter more than the year before, and it has raised its revenue outlook. It has also talked about expanding capacity by around thirty percent a year in 2027 and 2028. Even so, some analysts argue the company itself has become part of the bottleneck, simply because demand is so strong. And ASML isn't alone. Applied Materials, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron and KLA make other critical tools, and reports in 2026 suggest their delivery times have stretched sharply, in some cases to one and a half to two times what they were.

“ You can print money faster than you can print a new chip factory. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

Equipment Makers Have Their Own Shortages

One of the more counterintuitive findings from industry coverage is that equipment makers aren't short of willingness or money to expand. What they lack are components and raw materials of their own. A chip-making machine is made of thousands of precise parts, and if one supplier slips, the whole machine waits.

It's a reminder that the semiconductor industry is a chain of chains. Slow down a single link, whether a specialty gas, an optical element or a vacuum component, and the delay ripples upward. Building a new supplier takes years, not months.

The Packaging and Memory Squeeze

Making the silicon is only half the job. Advanced AI processors have to be packaged together with memory, and the process most associated with this is TSMC's CoWoS, short for Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate. Industry sources have described CoWoS capacity as oversubscribed through at least 2026, and Nvidia has publicly said the same about its own needs.

The memory side is just as tight. High-bandwidth memory, or HBM, is stacked tightly next to AI processors, and memory makers such as SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron have reported that their output is largely allocated well in advance. SK Hynix has even said the DRAM market is expected to stay short through 2026, especially at the high end.

The consequence is that a chip designer can have a brilliant design, a wafer booked at the foundry, and still wait, because the packaging line or the memory stack isn't available. That is why many analysts now say the real constraint has moved from the wafer to everything that comes after it.

Bottlenecks Beyond the Machines

  • Skilled people. Building and running a fab needs thousands of specialized engineers and technicians, and the talent pool is thin in many regions.
  • Power and water. Advanced factories consume large amounts of both, and local infrastructure has to keep up.
  • Construction time. A new fab typically takes years from groundbreaking to meaningful output.
  • Cleanroom capacity. Even when equipment arrives, there must be a qualified space ready to install and calibrate it.
  • Qualification. New lines have to be tested and proven before they make sellable chips, which adds months more.

The Geopolitical Layer

Semiconductors are now a matter of national strategy. The United States, Europe, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, China and India are all investing heavily in domestic chip capacity. TSMC alone has committed to a very large US investment as it expands outside Taiwan, and countries such as South Korea are planning big industrial clusters.

Yet money doesn't bypass the equipment queue. Korean industry reports have raised the possibility that securing advanced equipment could become a major variable in expansion plans, even as some officials say it is too early to call the situation a bottleneck. Subsidies like the US CHIPS Act help build factories, but they don't instantly produce lithography machines or packaging lines. Export controls add another complication, because rules on what can be sold to whom change where equipment can go.

“ A chip factory is a promise that takes years to keep. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

What This Means for Buyers, Businesses and Builders

If you buy computers, phones or cloud services, the effects are often indirect but real. When advanced memory and processors are scarce, prices for related components can rise, and some products launch in smaller quantities. Companies that rely on AI infrastructure may find they have to wait for capacity or pay a premium to secure it.

For businesses planning technology purchases, a few practical habits help:

  1. Order earlier. Lead times for servers and specialized hardware can be long, so build them into your timeline.
  2. Stay flexible. Where possible, qualify more than one supplier or configuration.
  3. Use what you have. Squeeze more from existing hardware with better software and scheduling before adding more.
  4. Watch the memory market. Memory pricing often shows tightness before it appears elsewhere.

Is Relief on the Way?

There are reasons for cautious optimism. TSMC is spending heavily on new capacity, and its guidance for 2026 capital spending sits in the tens of billions of dollars. ASML plans meaningful capacity growth over the next couple of years. Memory makers are expanding, and new packaging lines are coming online.

But expect relief to arrive in stages, not all at once, and expect the bottleneck to move around. When one constraint eases, attention often shifts to the next weakest link. A reasonable reading of current forecasts is that the tightest conditions will last through 2027, with gradual improvement afterward if demand doesn't outrun the new supply. Treat that as an informed estimate rather than a certainty, because demand for AI is the biggest unknown of all.

A Simple Way to Picture a Chip's Journey

Imagine ordering a custom-built car where every part comes from a different specialist, and each specialist has a waiting list. A modern AI chip is similar. A design team creates the blueprint. A foundry like TSMC prints it onto silicon wafers using lithography machines. Separate suppliers make the memory. Then the pieces are packaged together, tested, and shipped to a server maker who assembles them into systems for data centers.

Every one of those steps has its own capacity, its own lead time and its own risks. A delay in any stage holds up everything after it. That is why you can read headlines about record demand and record investment in the same week as stories about shortages. Both can be true, because spending money is much faster than building the physical capacity that the money is meant to buy.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is causing the semiconductor equipment shortage?

Strong AI-driven demand for advanced chips, combined with long lead times for lithography and other tools and limits in the supply chains of the equipment makers themselves.

What is a chip manufacturing bottleneck?

It is a single stage in the production process, such as lithography, packaging or memory supply, that limits how many finished chips can be made no matter how strong other stages are.

Why is ASML so important?

ASML is the only company that makes EUV lithography machines, which are essential for producing the most advanced chips.

How long will the shortage last?

Analysts such as Omdia expect bottlenecks to persist into 2027, though timing depends on how fast new capacity comes online and how AI demand evolves.

Key Takeaways • Chip Manufacturing Bottlenecks

Today's shortage is concentrated in advanced AI chips, not everyday components.

Equipment makers like ASML face their own component and capacity limits.

Packaging and high-bandwidth memory are as tight as chip fabrication itself.

Money alone cannot shorten the years it takes to build fabs and tools.

Expect gradual relief, with the bottleneck shifting from one link to the next.

The Chip Squeeze at a Glance

Figures drawn from 2026 industry reporting
60+ Planned ASML EUV Shipments
~30% Planned Yearly ASML Capacity Growth
2027 Bottlenecks Expected to Persist

Bottom Line: “The limit on AI is not ideas. It is how fast the world can build the machines that build the chips.”

title: Top 5 AI Video Generation Tools in 2026: Features, Free Plans and Who Each One Is For
subtitle: Google Veo, Runway, Kling, Luma and Pika compared by realism, control, free access and real-world use, plus prompting tips and the legal basics.
author: The Empire Insight Editorial Board
quotes: The best AI video tool is the one that fits your workflow, not the one that wins the loudest comparison chart.
Test two tools on the same prompt before you pay for either.
The tools do the rendering. You still supply the taste.
excerpt: AI video has finally become useful. We compare five leading tools, explain their free plans and limits, and show how to choose and prompt them well.
content:
Creator Guide 2026

A couple of years ago, AI video meant wobbly clips where hands melted and faces drifted. In 2026, you can type a sentence and get a short, believable scene, sometimes with synchronized sound. That jump has created a new problem: too many tools and too much hype. We looked at what the current top tier offers, how pricing and free plans work, and where each tool is strong or weak. Here are the top 5 AI video generation tools worth your attention, plus a clear way to choose between them.

How We Picked These Five

We weighed the things creators actually care about: how realistic the motion looks, how well the tool follows instructions, how much control you get, what the free tier lets you do, and how practical it is for real projects. We also leaned on a spread of recent comparisons and on the tools' own published information. One honest warning before we start: this category changes monthly. Features, credits and prices shift constantly, so always check each tool's official pricing page before paying for anything.

A quick note on a name you may be missing. OpenAI's Sora had a high profile, but multiple 2026 reports say OpenAI announced it would shut down its web and app experience in April 2026, with API access ending later in the year. If you're reading older tutorials that recommend it, treat them as out of date.

1. Google Veo 3.1: Best for Realistic Video With Sound

Veo is Google's video model, and the 3.1 version is widely regarded as one of the strongest overall options. Its headline strength is realism, including native audio, which means dialogue, ambient noise and effects can be generated along with the picture instead of added afterward. That matters more than it sounds. Matching sound to video is slow, fiddly work, and having it built in saves real time.

Best for: marketing clips, product concepts, and short story scenes where believability counts. Watch out for: access. Veo usually sits behind Google's paid AI plans or its developer platforms rather than a truly free tier, and clip length and resolution vary by plan.

2. Runway (Gen-4.5): Best for Creative Control

Runway has been in this space longer than most and thinks like a filmmaker's toolbox. You can generate from text or images, guide camera movement, extend clips, and edit within the same workspace. If you want to shape a result instead of rolling the dice, this is where many professionals end up.

Best for: filmmakers, designers and agencies who need consistency and editing tools. Watch out for: credits. Generation uses a credit system, and serious projects can burn through them quickly, so plan your prompts before you spend.

3. Kling AI (3.0): Best Value and Generous Free Access

Kling, from Chinese tech company Kuaishou, has earned a reputation for strong motion and good value. Its free tier gives you daily credits, and its paid plans start low compared with many rivals, which makes it a natural place to experiment. It handles movement and human action particularly well, and it is popular for turning still images into moving clips.

Best for: social content, image-to-video work and anyone on a tight budget. Watch out for: free outputs may carry restrictions such as watermarks, queue times can be longer on free plans, and you should read the terms on data and commercial use carefully.

“ The best AI video tool is the one that fits your workflow, not the one that wins the loudest comparison chart. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

4. Luma Dream Machine: Best for Cinematic Camera Moves

Luma's Dream Machine is known for a cinematic feel, with smooth camera motion and an easy interface. It is particularly good at taking a single image and bringing it to life, which makes it a favorite for visual artists, photographers and anyone with strong still imagery they want to animate.

Best for: mood pieces, music visuals, and animating existing artwork or photos. Watch out for: free access is limited to a small number of generations, so it works better as a test drive than as a full production plan.

5. Pika: Best for Quick, Fun Short-Form Clips

Pika leans into speed and playfulness. It offers creative effects and quick transformations that suit short, shareable videos for social platforms. It isn't trying to be a full film studio, and that's part of its charm. You can get a lively clip in minutes without learning a complicated interface.

Best for: social media creators, meme-style content and experiments. Watch out for: if you need long, highly realistic or tightly controlled footage, you will likely hit its limits and want one of the tools above.

Quick Comparison

  • Realism and sound: Google Veo 3.1
  • Control and editing: Runway Gen-4.5
  • Price-to-quality and free access: Kling AI
  • Cinematic image-to-video: Luma Dream Machine
  • Fast, fun short-form clips: Pika

Honorable mentions include PixVerse, Hailuo and Seedance for generation, and HeyGen and Synthesia if what you really need is a talking presenter or training video rather than cinematic footage.

How to Choose the Right Tool

  1. Start with the job. A product ad, a music visual and a classroom explainer need very different things.
  2. Test on free tiers first. Use the same prompt in two or three tools and compare, instead of trusting reviews alone.
  3. Check the license. Confirm whether your plan allows commercial use and whether watermarks are removed.
  4. Plan your workflow. Most polished results combine a generator, an editor, and separate music or voice work.

Getting Better Results: Prompting Tips That Actually Help

You don't need magic words, but structure helps. Describe the subject, the action, the setting, the camera and the mood, in that order. "A fisherman pulls a net at dawn, wide shot, slow push-in, soft fog, quiet and calm" will beat "cool fishing video" almost every time.

Keep each clip short and focused on one action. Most tools still struggle with complicated scenes and long continuous takes. It is usually better to generate several simple shots and stitch them together in an editor. Add details about lighting and lens, and avoid asking for readable text in the scene, which remains unreliable.

The Legal and Ethical Basics

AI video comes with responsibilities, and ignoring them can cost you. Here is the short version.

  • Read the terms. Rights to use and sell the output depend on the tool and your plan.
  • Don't imitate real people without permission. Faces, voices and likenesses raise serious legal and ethical issues.
  • Avoid copyrighted characters and brands. Generating them can create infringement problems even if the tool allows the prompt.
  • Disclose when it matters. Many platforms require labels for realistic synthetic content, and audiences increasingly expect honesty.
  • Be careful with sensitive topics. Realistic fake footage of news events can mislead people.

Laws on AI-generated content are still developing and differ by country, so when a project has real money or reputation at stake, it is worth asking a qualified professional.

Where AI Video Is Headed

The trajectory is clear: longer clips, better consistency between shots, tighter control over characters and camera, and sound that works out of the box. The gap between a beginner and a professional is shifting from technical skill to taste, storytelling and editing judgment. The tools do more of the typing. You still have to decide what is worth saying.

If you are just starting, pick one free tool, make five small experiments this week, and see what you enjoy. That beats reading another ranking, including this one.

Practical Ways to Use These Tools Right Now

The best use cases are often smaller than the hype suggests. A small shop can make a ten-second product teaser without hiring a crew. A teacher can turn a still diagram into a short animation that explains a concept. A musician can create visuals for a track on a tiny budget. A nonprofit can mock up a campaign video to test an idea before investing in a full shoot.

Another strong use is pre-visualization. Directors and designers can quickly sketch scenes, test camera angles and show clients a rough version before spending on production. In each case, the AI clip is a draft or a building block. The final polish, the story, the voiceover and the judgment about what to leave out still come from a person, and that is usually what separates a forgettable clip from a memorable one.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best AI video generator in 2026?

It depends on the job. Google Veo 3.1 is often praised for realism and sound, Runway for control, Kling for value, Luma for cinematic image-to-video, and Pika for quick social clips.

Are there free AI video generators?

Yes. Kling, Luma and Runway offer limited free access, though free plans usually restrict credits, length or quality and may add watermarks.

Can I use AI-generated videos commercially?

Often yes on paid plans, but it depends on each tool's terms. Always read the license and avoid copyrighted characters, brands or real people's likenesses.

What happened to Sora?

Reports in 2026 say OpenAI announced it would discontinue Sora's web and app experiences in April, with API access ending later in the year. Check OpenAI's official announcements for the latest.

Key Takeaways • Top 5 AI Video Tools

Veo, Runway, Kling, Luma and Pika each win at something different.

Free tiers are best for testing, not for heavy production.

Short, focused clips and clear prompts give the best results.

Check licensing, watermarks and likeness rules before publishing anything.

The tools do the rendering. You still supply the taste.

Kling Best Value

Bottom Line: “Test two tools on the same prompt before you pay for either.”

title: How Jensen Huang, Rene Haas, Andy Jassy, Satya Nadella and Dylan Field Are Shaping the AI Economy in 2026
shortTitle: The Leaders Behind the AI Economy
subtitle: From Nvidia's AI factories and Arm's data center push to Amazon's chip bet, Microsoft's Maia 300 and Figma's design-first view, here is how five leaders are building the AI era.
author: The Empire Insight Editorial Board
quotes: The AI race is no longer won by the best model alone. It is won by whoever can run it cheaply, at scale, every day.
When anyone can generate code, the scarce skill becomes knowing what is worth building.
AI has shifted from a software contest to an infrastructure race built on chips, power and cloud capacity.
Efficiency, not hype, will decide who wins the next phase of the AI economy.
The next AI winners will be the ones who make intelligence cheaper to run.
excerpt: AI is no longer just about chatbots. It is about chips, power and cloud contracts. Here is what Jensen Huang, Rene Haas, Andy Jassy, Satya Nadella and Dylan Field are each doing to shape the AI economy in 2026.
content:
Technology Insight 2026

Two years ago, the AI conversation was mostly about chatbots. Today it is about power grids, chip supply, cloud contracts and who gets to run the world's AI workloads at the lowest cost. The people steering that shift are not a single club. They run very different companies, and they disagree on plenty. But five of them, Jensen Huang, Rene Haas, Andy Jassy, Satya Nadella and Dylan Field, each hold a piece of the puzzle. This is a plain-English look at what each one is doing in October 2026, and what it adds up to for the rest of us.

The AI Story Has Moved From Software to Infrastructure

For a while, AI looked like a software race. Whoever had the cleverest model won the headlines. That has quietly changed. Models still matter, but the bottleneck now sits underneath them: chips, memory, electricity and data center space. Industry estimates cited this year put big-cloud spending on AI infrastructure in the hundreds of billions of dollars for 2026 alone, far above 2025.

That is why this list of names makes sense. One builds the dominant AI hardware. One designs the processor architecture inside a huge share of the world's devices and servers. Two run cloud platforms that are racing to build their own silicon. And one leads the design platform where many of the resulting products get shaped. Read together, they show how the AI economy is actually being assembled.

Jensen Huang: Selling the “AI Factory”

Nvidia's founder and CEO has spent the past year repeating one idea in different ways: AI is not a feature, it is infrastructure. At CES 2026, he argued that companies are not printing new money to buy Nvidia systems. They are redirecting budgets that used to go to conventional servers into what he calls AI factories. It is a clever reframing, because it turns a scary capital bill into a replacement cycle.

At GTC in March, Nvidia introduced its Vera Rubin rack-scale platform, and Huang told the audience that revenue visibility for its current and upcoming AI systems could reach at least $1 trillion through 2027. On the February earnings call he said “compute equals revenues now,” his shorthand for why he thinks the spending is sustainable. Nvidia's market value was reported at around $4.3 trillion in early August.

Two other threads are worth watching. The first is “sovereign AI,” where governments fund their own national computing capacity. The second is physical AI, meaning robots and machines that act in the real world. Both widen the market beyond the usual cloud giants. The caution is that export rules on advanced chips and the push by customers to build their own silicon could trim Nvidia's lead over time. Huang's answer so far has been to keep selling complete systems rather than lone chips.

“ The AI race is no longer won by the best model alone. It is won by whoever can run it cheaply, at scale, every day. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

Rene Haas: Arm Steps Out of the Phone and Into the Data Center

Arm built its reputation in smartphones, where its low-power designs are everywhere. Under CEO Rene Haas, the company is deliberately moving toward cloud and AI data centers. He has said as much, describing a shift away from being known mainly for phones. The logic is simple: when data centers run into power limits, efficiency becomes the thing everyone wants.

Haas's most interesting argument is about the humble CPU. As AI shifts from single prompts to agents that run continuously, someone has to manage memory, call tools, query databases and keep the whole system moving. That work mostly lands on CPUs, not GPUs. Arm says that makes processor cores more valuable, not less, and that the world will need several times more cores within the same power budget.

The numbers Arm shared this year back that story up. The company said data center royalty revenue more than doubled year on year in its latest quarter, that shipments of its Neoverse cores passed 1.5 billion, and that customer demand for its new Arm AGI CPU has gone past $2 billion across fiscal 2027 and 2028. That last product matters for another reason. It signals that Arm is not only licensing designs anymore but also offering finished silicon, a real change in its business model. Haas has said partners he checked with were supportive, though it is fair to note that some customers may still feel uneasy about a supplier moving closer to being a competitor.

Arm's own executives also point out that over half of the new cloud computing capacity added in the past twelve months ran on Arm-based processors. Amazon's Graviton and the in-house chips at Google and Microsoft all build on the architecture. In other words, Haas does not need to beat the cloud giants. He just needs to be inside what they build.

Andy Jassy: Amazon's $200 Billion Bet on Its Own Chips

Of the five, Andy Jassy has made the boldest public wager in dollars. Amazon said it plans roughly $200 billion in capital spending in 2026, mostly aimed at AI and infrastructure. In his April shareholder letter he explained the thinking: AWS's AI business had reached a $15 billion annual run rate, and he said a large share of the planned spending already had customer commitments behind it.

The heart of the plan is custom silicon. Amazon's Graviton CPUs and Trainium AI chips are being positioned as a cheaper path than relying only on Nvidia. Jassy said Trainium should save Amazon tens of billions of dollars in capital spending each year and give it a margin edge on inference. He also said the chips business was running at more than $20 billion a year and growing at triple-digit rates.

Demand shows up in the deals. In April, Amazon agreed to invest up to $25 billion more in Anthropic, which in turn committed to spend over $100 billion on AWS over ten years and secured access to as much as 5 gigawatts of capacity on Amazon's custom chips. Reports also describe a Trainium commitment from OpenAI beginning in 2027. Amazon has also deepened its relationship with Nvidia, so this is not a simple either-or story.

The risk is obvious. A $200 billion year only pays off if customers keep showing up and if the chips deliver the promised savings. Jassy's reply is that the cloud industry has been through a similar build-then-fill cycle before, and he likes how it turned out.

Satya Nadella: Microsoft Wants More Choice, Not Fewer Suppliers

Microsoft's approach under Satya Nadella is best described as “build your own, but keep buying.” The company launched its Maia 200 inference chip in January and, on October 12, unveiled Maia 300, its third-generation design. Microsoft says Maia 300 should deliver about 40% more AI output per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems, with deployments starting in 2027. Nadella described it publicly as the company's biggest bet yet on its own silicon.

The reasoning is cost. Microsoft has told investors that running OpenAI and in-house models on Maia 200 lowers operating costs by roughly 30% to 40% compared with top-end Nvidia hardware, according to reporting this summer. Maia 200 already supports Copilot, and GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry are expected to follow by year-end.

But Nadella has been clear that this does not mean Microsoft is leaving Nvidia or AMD. The company's fleet is deliberately mixed. Analysts also note that Maia is expected to represent only a modest slice of Microsoft's total AI chip spending in early 2027, even though capital spending is reported to run above $175 billion a year. So the practical story is leverage. Having a credible in-house option improves Microsoft's bargaining position and its margins, without betting everything on one design.

Nadella has also raised an issue many CEOs avoid: trust. He has suggested treating powerful AI models as potential insider risks, assuming they could make mistakes or be compromised, and building containment from the start. For businesses deploying AI agents, that is a useful and slightly uncomfortable piece of advice.

Dylan Field: The Layer Where Products Get Their Personality

Dylan Field sits at the opposite end of the stack. Figma makes no chips. It makes the software where teams design and now increasingly build products. That is exactly why his view is valuable. If AI makes code cheap and fast to produce, what separates one product from another?

Field's answer is design, taste and a clear point of view. Speaking at Config India in Bengaluru this month, he said design is increasingly what sets products apart as code becomes commoditized, and that he does not expect AI to cause designer job losses. He also noted that India is now Figma's second-largest market by daily usage.

The company's numbers suggest AI is helping rather than hurting. Figma reported second-quarter revenue of $370 million, up 48% from a year earlier, with growth accelerating for a third straight quarter. Its prompt-to-app tool, Figma Make, can now work directly inside production codebases, and the company reports that more than 80% of larger paid customers were using its AI credits weekly by the end of June. Figma has also been opening its platform to outside AI agents through MCP, with new partners added this month.

It is not all smooth. Figma said it is searching for a new CTO, with its AI and editor engineering teams reporting directly to Field in the meantime. Still, his central bet is worth taking seriously: when everyone can generate software, the winners will be the teams with better judgment about what to build.

“ When anyone can generate code, the scarce skill becomes knowing what is worth building. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

Where These Five Leaders Agree and Disagree

Put side by side, a few patterns stand out.

  • Efficiency is the new currency. Haas talks about performance per watt, Nadella about output per megawatt, Jassy about cost per inference. Even Huang's pitch rests on getting more work out of every unit of power.
  • Nobody wants a single supplier. Amazon and Microsoft are building chips while still buying from Nvidia. Arm sits underneath many of them. The market is becoming layered, not winner-takes-all.
  • Agents change the hardware story. Always-on AI agents lean heavily on CPUs, memory and networking, which is why Arm, Amazon and Nvidia are all talking about them.
  • The money has to show up. Huang says demand converts to revenue. Jassy points to customer commitments. Field points to paying customers using AI credits. The skeptics want proof, and so far each leader is offering numbers rather than promises.

Where they differ is on who captures the value. Huang believes it flows to integrated systems. Jassy and Nadella believe owning more of the stack improves margins. Haas wants to be the common foundation under everyone. Field believes value drifts up to design and product thinking. All four can be partly right at once, and that is what makes the next two years interesting.

What This Means for Businesses and Small Teams

You do not need a data center to benefit from any of this. The competition among these companies tends to push the price of AI down and the quality up. A few practical takeaways:

  1. Expect cheaper AI over time. Custom chips and heavy competition should reduce the cost of running AI tools, but plan for price changes rather than assuming they are fixed.
  2. Avoid locking yourself in too early. With so many platforms racing, flexible contracts and portable workflows are safer than a long commitment to one vendor.
  3. Invest in judgment, not just tools. If software gets easier to produce, your edge comes from understanding your customers and having a clear point of view.
  4. Treat AI agents with care. Give them limited access, review what they do and keep humans in charge of sensitive decisions.
  5. Watch energy and capacity news. Power availability is becoming a real limit on AI growth, and it will shape pricing and availability.

The Bottom Line

Nobody can say for certain how this plays out. Spending is enormous, forecasts are bold, and some of the numbers come from the companies themselves, so a healthy dose of skepticism is reasonable. But the direction is clear. The AI economy is being built layer by layer, from silicon to cloud to the design tools that shape the final product, and each of these five leaders is pulling hard on a different layer. The smartest move for everyone else is to keep learning, stay flexible and pay attention to the economics underneath the headlines.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who are the key leaders shaping AI infrastructure in 2026?

Jensen Huang of Nvidia, Rene Haas of Arm, Andy Jassy of Amazon, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Dylan Field of Figma each influence a different layer, from chips and cloud to design software.

Why are Amazon and Microsoft building their own AI chips?

Mainly to lower costs, reduce dependence on a single supplier and improve margins. Both still buy chips from other vendors, so the goal is more choice rather than full replacement.

What is Arm's role in the AI boom?

Arm designs the processor architecture that many cloud and device chips are based on. It is expanding into data centers and has launched its own AGI CPU as AI agents increase demand for efficient processors.

How is Jensen Huang shaping the AI economy?

Through Nvidia's complete AI systems, including the Vera Rubin platform, and by arguing that AI spending is a redirection of existing infrastructure budgets toward “AI factories.”

Where does Figma fit into AI strategy?

Figma focuses on the product layer. Its tools help teams design and build with AI, and CEO Dylan Field argues that design and taste become the main differentiators as code gets easier to generate.

AI has shifted from a software contest to an infrastructure race built on chips, power and cloud capacity.

Amazon and Microsoft are building custom chips to cut costs, while still buying from Nvidia and AMD.

Arm is moving from phones into data centers as AI agents increase demand for efficient CPUs.

Figma's bet is that design and judgment matter more as code becomes cheaper to produce.

Efficiency, not hype, will decide who wins the next phase of the AI economy.
